messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mr. Singh, a 64-year-old South Asian male, has been experiencing significant distress since his captivity experience two years ago. Married and working at a warehouse, Mr. Singh's life changed dramatically after the traumatic event that occurred one evening at around 8 PM. Since then, he has found himself in a cycle of fear and avoidance that has increasingly impacted both his work and personal life. At work, where the day shifts start late, the same time of day when the captivity began triggers intense anxiety for Mr. Singh. As the clock approaches 8 PM, he finds it difficult to concentrate on his tasks, often feeling as if the threat is looming again. This has led him to engage in maladaptive strategies such as avoiding sleep and frequently checking his surroundings for any signs of danger. The same time of day also evokes vivid memories of that evening, making it hard for him to function normally. One night, while watching a documentary about snakes on television, Mr. Singh was suddenly overwhelmed by the memory of encountering a snake during his captivity. This trigger has made him extremely anxious about any mention or visual representation of snakes, causing him to avoid watching TV programs and movies that might feature them. He is constantly vigilant, checking behind him and around corners, believing that he must remain hyperalert to prevent another traumatic event from occurring. Mr. Singh’s wife has noticed his distress and frequently finds herself reassuring him that he is safe at home, but even this does not seem to alleviate his anxiety. His constant body monitoring and reassurance-seeking behaviors have become a part of their daily routine. The fear of another attack has made Mr. Singh feel helpless and convinced that bad things are inevitable. He believes that if he thinks too much about the event, he will not be able to handle it, which further reinforces his avoidance behaviors. Mr. Singh’s nighttime vigilance is particularly troubling. Lying in bed at night, he constantly checks for signs of danger, making it difficult for him to fall asleep or remain asleep. His wife has observed that his sleep disturbances have become more frequent and severe over time. This lack of sleep exacerbates his anxiety, causing him to feel even less secure during the day. The experience of captivity has left Mr. Singh with a pervasive sense that life may not be worth living anymore. He often feels overwhelmed by the idea that he cannot prevent bad things from happening again. These negative appraisals have deepened his hypervigilance and reinforced his belief that the world is unsafe, particularly at night. Over time, these maladaptive strategies have compounded his distress. Mr. Singh’s constant checking for danger and avoidance of sleep have led to significant disruptions in his daily life. His relationship with his wife has also been strained as he relies heavily on her reassurances, which can feel burdensome for both of them. The cumulative effect of these behaviors has made it harder for him to engage in normal activities without feeling threatened or anxious. Mr. Singh finally sought help after realizing that his symptoms were worsening and affecting his ability to work and maintain a stable relationship with his wife. He is most afraid of the constant fear and vigilance that control his life, but he is also hopeful that through therapy, he can regain some sense of normalcy and feel more secure in his daily routines.
